title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In heavy building materials, whoever solves the last mile for bulky freight owns the margin.
epigraph.author: Supply Chain First Principles

web_blocks.title: 3.1 Store Footprint, Owned Real Estate Fortress & Supply Chain Architecture

web_blocks.html: Lowe's physical moat rests on a nationwide retail store footprint. It ended FY2025 with 1,759 U.S. stores and outlets, expanding to 1,762 stores (197.0 million indoor selling square feet) by October 30, 2026 [1, 2]. Each standard store averages 112,000 indoor square feet plus a 32,000-square-foot garden center, open daily across all 50 states [1]. Store density peaks in Texas (151 stores), Florida (132), North Carolina (116), California (112), Ohio (84), and Pennsylvania (83) [1]. Item 2 of the FY2025 Form 10-K confirms a major advantage: roughly 89% of Lowe's retail stores are owned (including buildings on leased land) [1]. Only about 11% are leased from third-party landlords [1]. That ownership kept occupancy costs at just $1,932 million, or 2.30% of Retail Home Improvement sales in FY2025 [1]. It shields margins from rent inflation and provides durable balance-sheet collateral [1].

Behind the stores sits a modern, multi-tiered logistics network. It spans over 120 supply chain sites and more than 65 million square feet of capacity [1, 2, 13]. Over 540 newly acquired Pro branches from Foundation Building Materials and Artisan Design Group now supplement that base [1, 2, 13]. Each facility type matches specific freight physics [13]. Regional Distribution Centers (RDCs) group fast-moving boxed goods from domestic and global vendors for rapid store restocking. Flatbed Distribution Centers (FDCs) and Flatbed Fulfillment Centers (FFCs) handle heavy lumber, plywood, drywall, shingles, and rebar [13]. They ship directly to Pro jobsites without clogging retail store yards [13]. Coastal Holding Facilities and Import Distribution Centers absorb seasonal and trans-Pacific container surges before routing freight inland [13].

web_blocks.title: 3.2 Market Delivery Model (MDM), Omnichannel Fulfillment & Working Capital Cycle

web_blocks.html: Completing the Market Delivery Model (MDM) in 2023–2024 was one of Marvin Ellison's best operational upgrades [13]. In the past, Lowe's stored bulky appliances, riding mowers, grills, and patio sets in cramped store backrooms. That practice tied up working capital, increased handling damage, and forced store staff to manage local truck deliveries. Under MDM, appliances, water heaters, generators, and riding mowers ship from Bulk Distribution Centers through local cross-dock hubs straight to homes [13]. That shift freed store backroom space, cut damage claims, and lifted inventory turns [13]. It also enabled next-day or two-day appliance delivery across major metros, driving Lowe's eighth straight quarter of positive Appliances comps in Q3 FY2026 [13, 24].

Lowe's has also turned its 1,762 stores into local omnichannel fulfillment hubs. Roughly 60% of online orders fill directly from stores via BOPIS lockers, curbside pickup, or gig-economy same-day delivery [13, 14]. Parcel stores and Online Fulfillment Centers handle direct-to-home shipments [13, 14]. Online sales growth hit +17.4% year-over-year in Q3 FY2026—its fifth straight double-digit quarter and third straight above 15% [2, 14, 24]. Lowe's first-in-sector third-party marketplace and AI assistant 'Mylow' fueled that digital surge [2, 14, 24]. On working capital, home improvement turns slower than grocery clubs like Costco because stores carry 40,000+ SKUs, including slow-moving valves, fasteners, and lumber. At FY2025 year-end, Lowe's held $17,300 million in inventory against $9,762 million in payables—a $7,538 million net spread [1]. That equals roughly 3.3x annual inventory turns (~110 days on hand) and ~62 days payable [1]. Still, tight inventory control generated a $703 million working-capital cash inflow in FY2025 [1]. Accounts receivable rose from $94 million to $1,090 million (and $1,256 million by October 30, 2026) purely because FBM and ADG extend B2B trade credit [1, 2].

web_blocks.title: 3.3 FY2025 Audited Revenue-to-Free-Cash-Flow Waterfall ($100 Unit Economics)

web_blocks.html: To see how Lowe's store-level economics convert sales into owner cash, the table below traces every $100 of audited FY2025 revenue down to free cash flow [1]. This single-year audit shows why merchandise margin discipline and light 2.6% capital intensity sustain high cash conversion even when housing demand stalls [1].

web_blocks.title: Freight & Fuel Sensitivity: Why Q3 FY2026 Gross Margin Compressed 124 Basis Points
paragraphs: Even a modern supply chain remains exposed to freight costs and mix shifts. In Q3 FY2026, gross margin fell 124 basis points year-over-year from 34.19% to 32.95% ($7,497 million on $22,756 million of sales) [2, 9].

Three concrete forces drove that drop [2, 9]. Diesel and transport costs jumped 15% sequentially from Q2. Lower-margin FBM/ADG wholesale sales plus promo appliances and outdoor gear also diluted mix. Finally, Lowe's reinvested about two-thirds of its $250 million IEEPA tariff refund into Q4 customer value and loyalty offers [2, 9].

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand why Amazon has never been able to crush Lowe's the way it devastated bookstores, electronics chains, and department stores, you and I have to talk about physics and real estate. Try shipping a 40-pound bag of concrete mix, twelve sheets of half-inch plywood, or a 300-pound French-door refrigerator through a standard parcel carrier. The freight economics collapse immediately. Home improvement is a heavy, bulky, urgent business, and Lowe's has spent the last three decades anchoring its physical moat in the ground.

At the end of October 2026, Lowe's operated 1,762 retail stores across all 50 states, each averaging roughly 112,000 square feet indoors plus a 32,000-square-foot garden center. Here is a balance-sheet fortress that most casual observers miss: according to Item 2 of Lowe's FY2025 Form 10-K, approximately 89% of those retail stores are owned by Lowe's (including buildings on leased land), with only 11% leased from third-party landlords. That ownership keeps occupancy and facility expenses at just 2.30% of retail sales—shielding Lowe's from the aggressive rent escalations that squeeze leased mall and strip-center retailers.

Behind those stores, Marvin Ellison's team spent six years rebuilding a fragmented supply chain into a specialized network of more than 120 logistics facilities covering 65 million square feet. The crown jewel of that overhaul is the Market Delivery Model, completed nationwide in 2024. For decades, Lowe's crammed refrigerators, washers, and riding mowers into store backrooms, damaging inventory and wasting associate labor. Today, those bulky items bypass the store entirely, flowing from regional Bulk Distribution Centers through local cross-dock terminals straight into a homeowner's kitchen or garage. Meanwhile, Flatbed Distribution Centers dispatch lumber and drywall directly to contractor jobsites, and over 60% of Lowe's fast-growing online orders—up 17.4% in Q3 FY2026—are picked up right at the local store or delivered same-day via gig networks.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Follow Every $100 Through the Cash Register
book_callouts.text: In FY2025, out of every $100 rung up at Lowe's, $66.52 paid for merchandise, $19.46 covered store payroll, marketing, and overhead, and $2.25 went to depreciation and amortization—leaving $11.77 in GAAP operating profit. After $1.63 in net interest and $2.43 in taxes, net earnings stood at $7.71. Yet because Lowe's spends just $2.56 per $100 on capital expenditures and generates strong non-cash add-backs, it kept $8.87 per $100 in pure Free Cash Flow—$7.65 billion in a single housing-trough year.

book_subsections.title: The Friction Points: Slower Traffic, Diesel Spikes, and New Trade Credit Risk
paragraphs: An honest forensic audit never stops at the strengths. When you and I examine Lowe's store-level unit economics over the past three years, two subtle yellow flags jump off the page. First, retail customer transactions have declined three years in a row—falling from 827 million in FY2023 to 801 million in FY2024 and 780 million in FY2025, with another 1.7% drop in Q3 FY2026. Positive comparable sales have been carried entirely by higher average tickets ($106.13 in FY2025, up from $102.47 in FY2023) and surging e-commerce. A retailer can lean on ticket size for a while, but lasting operating leverage eventually requires more shoppers walking through the doors.

Second, physical scale does not immunize Lowe's from freight inflation or working-capital evolution. In Q3 FY2026, a 15% sequential spike in diesel costs, combined with promotional appliance sales and the lower-margin wholesale mix of FBM and ADG, compressed consolidated gross margin by 124 basis points to 32.95%. At the same time, acquiring FBM and ADG introduced a brand-new working-capital dynamic: accounts receivable jumped more than tenfold from $94 million in FY2024 to $1,090 million at FY2025 year-end and $1,256 million by October 2026. Retail shoppers pay with a credit card at the register; commercial framing contractors buy on 30-to-60-day trade credit. Managing that commercial credit book through the next construction downturn will test a muscle Lowe's has never had to flex at this scale.

book_subsections.title: Why 89% Real Estate Ownership and 3.3x Inventory Turns Define the Cash Engine
paragraphs: If you compare Lowe's unit economics to a grocery warehouse club like Costco, the contrast teaches you a profound lesson about retail physics. Costco stocks fewer than 4,000 fast-moving SKUs, turns its inventory 11 to 12 times a year, and earns a razor-thin 11% merchandise gross margin. Lowe's sits at the exact opposite end of the spectrum: a single Lowe's superstore must stock over 40,000 SKUs—from 50-cent brass plumbing elbows that might sell twice a month to pallets of seasonal mulch and $3,000 smart refrigerators. Consequently, Lowe's turns its $17.3 billion inventory roughly 3.3 times a year (about 110 days on hand) against 62 days of accounts payable. That means Lowe's cannot rely on negative working capital to fund its growth the way a grocer does; instead, it earns a fat 33.48% gross margin—three times Costco's merchandise markup—to compensate for carrying slow-turning depth.

What turns that 33.48% gross margin into an extraordinary $7.65 billion Free Cash Flow machine is capital intensity—or rather, the lack of it once a national store network is mature. Because Lowe's already owns roughly 89% of its 1,762 stores, it does not need to spend $6 billion a year building hundreds of new boxes or fighting landlords on rent resets. Total capital expenditures in FY2025 were just $2,213 million—a modest 2.56% of revenue—directed primarily toward store resets, front-end self-checkout lanes, AI replenishment software, and supply-chain automation. Even with FY2026 capex guided up to $2.5 billion to support FBM's 15 new branches and IT modernization, capex absorbs barely a quarter of Lowe's nearly $10 billion in annual operating cash flow.

Think about what that means for your margin of safety as an investor. In a world where digital-only competitors bleed cash on parcel shipping for heavy goods, Lowe's turns its existing owned stores into last-mile pickup hubs—fulfilling roughly 60% of online orders right out of local inventory via BOPIS lockers, curbside pickup, and gig-economy same-day vans. Every incremental online order picked up at a Lowe's store leverages fixed real estate and store payroll that are already paid for. As long as management keeps shrink under control, manages diesel freight spikes through carrier contracts, and polices FBM's new $1.26 billion B2B receivables book with discipline, Lowe's unit-economic engine remains one of the sturdiest cash generators in American retail.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Low Maintenance Capex Is the Secret to 115% Cash Conversion
callouts.text: When a mature retail duopolist owns 89% of its real estate and needs only 2.5% to 2.7% of sales in annual capital expenditures to maintain and modernize its footprint, almost every dollar of accounting profit converts directly into distributable Free Cash Flow.
